title: 阅读模拟测试
goal: 完成词汇理解、长篇阅读和仔细阅读任务。

points.label: 完成词库选词并核对语境
为陈述匹配有依据的段落

sources.title: 全国大学英语四、六级考试大纲（2016年修订版）
sources.used: 阅读材料长度和作答形式

body.p: 阅读理解有词汇理解、长篇阅读和仔细阅读三类，各 10 题，共用 40 分钟。词汇理解从 15 个词的词库中选词。长篇阅读为每条陈述选出对应的段落。仔细阅读有 2 篇短文。
词汇理解的材料为 200–250 词，长篇阅读约 1000 词，仔细阅读每篇 300–350 词。本课程的仔细阅读每题设 4 个选项。

groups.text:
Word bank: available, balance, borrow, carefully, collect, crowded, damaged, discover, equipment, local, materials, prevent, repair, shared, tools

A neighborhood tool library allows residents to borrow equipment for short periods. A person who needs a ladder for one afternoon may have nowhere to store one for the rest of the year. In a collection (1) ______ by several households, the same object can be used at different times.

Before opening, volunteers asked residents what they would be likely to (2) ______. Their answers helped the organizers decide which items to obtain first. The library began with hand tools and later added larger pieces of (3) ______, including ladders. Each item receives a number so that staff can record when it leaves and when it is returned.

When an object comes back, a volunteer checks it (4) ______. If a handle is loose or a blade is (5) ______, the item is set aside. Someone with suitable skills may then (6) ______ it before it returns to the shelves. This process helps (7) ______ the use of unsafe items.

The library also holds short workshops. Participants learn how to choose the right (8) ______ for a job and how to look after them. A workshop might use simple (9) ______ such as wood and paper to demonstrate a task. The collection changes over time, but an online list shows which items are currently (10) ______ for borrowing.

items.why: several households 使用同一物品，shared 表示共用的。
前文说明居民借用工具，asked residents what they would be likely to borrow 指询问可能借用的物品。
including ladders 列举较大型的设备，pieces of equipment 表示设备。
下文检查松动或损坏，carefully 修饰 checks，表示仔细检查。
与 handle is loose 并列，damaged 描述刀刃受损的情况。
物品因松动或损坏被放在一旁，repair 表示将其修复后再上架。
检查和修复有助于防止使用不安全物品，prevent 符合此处的目的。
choose the right tools for a job 指为工作选择合适的工具，them 指代这些工具。
wood and paper 是材料，materials 概括这两个例子。
online list 显示当前可借的物品，available for borrowing 表示可以借用。

groups.text:
Keeping a Community Archive

[A] A community archive is a collection of records about a place and the people connected with it. Its holdings may include photographs, letters, maps and recordings. Unlike a collection formed around one famous person, it can bring together accounts of ordinary activities that rarely appear in official histories. An archive does more than accumulate old objects: it also records where they came from and makes them available in ways that respect the people represented. The choices made by organizers determine whose experiences can be found and understood by later visitors. The archive can also document changes that residents remember differently over time.

[B] The first challenge is deciding what the collection is meant to cover. An archive devoted to a neighborhood might choose a particular area and a period of time, while accepting that people move across boundaries. A written collecting policy helps volunteers judge whether an offered item belongs. Without such a policy, a small group may accept more than it can describe or store. A policy can be revised as the community changes, but a clear initial scope gives the group a useful basis for discussing new offers. It also helps donors understand why some records are sought before others.

[C] Invitations to contribute should reach beyond people who already attend local meetings. Organizers can visit workplaces, schools and clubs and explain what kinds of records might be useful. They may also offer conversations in languages used locally. These efforts take time, but they reduce dependence on a narrow circle of contacts. A collection built only through existing friendships may preserve those friendships very well while leaving out other experiences of the same place. Asking different groups what they want remembered can also change the organizers' first assumptions. Listening at an early stage can shape the direction of the collection.

[D] A donor may know details that are not visible in a photograph. The date, location and names of participants can turn an image into a useful record. Volunteers therefore ask contributors to describe items when they are offered, and write down the source of each description. If the date is uncertain, that uncertainty is recorded rather than replaced by a guess. A later visitor may supply new evidence, but the original information should remain distinguishable from the addition so that researchers can see how the account developed. Keeping the original description also allows future researchers to reconsider the evidence.

[E] Personal records can contain sensitive information. Before accepting a recording, an archive should discuss who may listen to it and whether parts need to remain closed for a period. A person's willingness to be interviewed is not necessarily permission to publish every detail online. The agreement should be recorded in language that contributors understand. Restrictions can make access less immediate, yet they can also make it possible to preserve accounts that people would otherwise be unwilling to share at all. The length and terms of each restriction should be clear to both parties.

[F] Physical storage calls for attention even when a collection is small. Papers should be kept in clean folders, away from direct sunlight and water. Volunteers can note the condition of an item when it arrives and check it again later. If a photograph is already torn, that fact belongs in the record; it should not be treated as damage caused during storage. Fragile objects may need advice from a trained conservator, because an attempt to mend them with ordinary tape can make future treatment harder. The group can seek professional guidance before attempting work on a fragile item.

[G] Digitizing an item creates another way to consult it, but a digital copy also needs care. Files should have consistent names and be stored in more than one location. A single copy on one computer may be lost if the machine fails. Staff must also check from time to time that files can still be opened with available software. Scanning does not remove the need to care for the original, which may contain details that are difficult to capture in an image. Digital storage therefore adds responsibilities even as it offers more ways to consult records.

[H] A catalog connects users with the collection. A useful entry identifies an item and describes its subject, date and source when these are known. Descriptions should use terms that visitors are likely to search for, while preserving information about older names when relevant. For example, a building may have changed its name several times. Including those names can help people find the same place even when they remember different periods. A catalog need not contain every detail to give a reader a reliable starting point. A visitor can then request the item to explore its contents more closely.

[I] Exhibitions give archives a way to share selected material, but selection involves interpretation. A display about a street market might pair sellers' photographs with customers' memories, showing how the same place served different people. Captions should distinguish an individual's recollection from a fact established by several records. When accounts disagree, a display can present the difference instead of forcing them into one story. Visitors can then understand both what the evidence shows and where the record remains incomplete. The choice of captions matters because visitors may not have access to the full records.

[J] Long-term work depends on more than an enthusiastic beginning. Volunteers leave, equipment wears out and storage costs continue. Writing down routine procedures helps new members take over tasks without relying entirely on one person's memory. Regular conversations with contributors can also reveal whether access rules and descriptions still meet their needs. An archive that reviews its practices can adjust to changing circumstances while keeping a clear record of its earlier decisions. Such continuity helps a collection remain useful beyond the people who first assembled it. Each generation of volunteers can contribute while learning from the decisions made before it.

items.stem: A record of an item's condition can distinguish earlier damage from damage during storage.
items.why: 第六段 note the condition of an item when it arrives，并说已有的破损 should not be treated as damage caused during storage。

items.stem: An archive can collect accounts of everyday life that official histories may overlook.
items.why: 第一段 accounts of ordinary activities that rarely appear in official histories 是依据，everyday life 改写 ordinary activities。

items.stem: Showing conflicting memories can make the limits of the evidence visible.
items.why: 第九段 When accounts disagree, a display can present the difference，观众由此看到 where the record remains incomplete。

items.stem: A written scope helps a small archive assess offers of material.
items.why: 第二段 A written collecting policy helps volunteers judge whether an offered item belongs 是依据，written scope 改写 collecting policy。

items.stem: Digital files need copies in separate places and checks on whether they remain readable.
items.why: 第七段 stored in more than one location 和 check from time to time that files can still be opened 分别对应陈述的两部分。

items.stem: A photograph's contributor may supply information that the image itself cannot show.
items.why: 第四段 A donor may know details that are not visible in a photograph，后面列出日期、地点和人名。

items.stem: Documenting routine work can help replacement volunteers continue the archive's activities.
items.why: 第十段 Writing down routine procedures helps new members take over tasks 是依据，replacement volunteers 改写 new members。

items.stem: Different names for one building can help users locate its records.
items.why: 第八段 a building may have changed its name several times，Including those names can help people find the same place。

items.stem: Speaking to groups outside existing networks may lead to a more inclusive collection.
items.why: 第三段 Invitations to contribute should reach beyond people who already attend local meetings。只靠熟人建成的收藏会 leaving out other experiences。

items.stem: Limits on access may encourage people to contribute accounts they would otherwise withhold.
items.why: 第五段 Restrictions ... make it possible to preserve accounts that people would otherwise be unwilling to share，withhold 改写 unwilling to share。

groups.text:
A Market's Returnable Containers

A town market recently tested a returnable container system for prepared food. Instead of receiving a disposable box with each purchase, customers could pay a small deposit for a durable container. When they brought it back to any participating stall, they received the deposit again. Stallholders then sent the containers to a central washing facility before they were used for another meal. The trial was designed to reduce the number of boxes discarded after a single use.

At first, the organizers measured success by counting how many containers were issued. That number rose steadily, but it did not reveal whether the containers were being returned. The team therefore began tracking returns as well. They found that many customers brought containers back within a week, while others kept them at home for longer. A container waiting in a cupboard cannot replace another disposable box until it reenters circulation.

To make returns easier, the market added a collection point near its main entrance. Previously, customers had to return containers directly to a participating stall, which could mean waiting in a queue. The new point accepted containers from all the stalls in the trial. It did not give an immediate cash refund; instead, customers received a receipt that could be exchanged for the deposit at a stall. This arrangement shortened the time needed to drop off a container, although it added a step for anyone who wanted the deposit back.

The organizers also considered the water and energy required for washing and transport. They did not assume that every reusable container automatically had a lower impact than every disposable one. The result depends partly on how often each container is reused and how efficiently it is cleaned. The trial's next stage will compare those factors as well as return rates. The market's experience suggests that a reusable system must be designed around the full journey of a container, not simply around the moment it is handed to a customer.

items.stem: What was the main purpose of the market's trial?
options: To reduce the number of food boxes used only once
To increase the number of containers issued
To replace the central washing facility with stall washing
To shorten the time needed to prepare each meal
items.why: 原文说试验旨在 reduce the number of boxes discarded after a single use，即第一项。

items.stem: Why did the organizers begin counting returns?
options: Customers had complained about waiting in queues at participating stalls.
The number issued did not show whether containers came back.
The washing facility could no longer accept used containers.
The deposit had already been removed from every purchase.
items.why: 原文说发出的数量 did not reveal whether the containers were being returned，即第二项。

items.stem: What changed when the entrance collection point was added?
options: Customers no longer needed a receipt to reclaim a deposit at any participating stall.
Each stall began accepting only its own containers.
Customers could leave containers without joining a stall queue.
The deposit was returned immediately at the entrance.
items.why: 原文对比了原先可能需要排队和入口收集点缩短交还时间，即第三项。

items.stem: What can be inferred about a container kept at home?
options: It has already been recorded as returned to the market.
It requires no further washing before the next meal.
It earns a refund without being taken to the market.
It cannot replace another box while it remains unused.
items.why: 原文说柜中的容器重新流通之前不能替代另一个一次性盒子，即第四项。

items.stem: What does the author emphasize in the final paragraph?
options: The number issued is the only useful measure of success.
The impact depends on reuse and cleaning, not only on returns.
Every reusable container has less impact than a disposable box.
Transport and washing have no role in the trial's next stage.
items.why: 原文指出影响取决于复用次数和清洗效率，下一阶段也比较回收率，即第二项。

groups.text:
Listening to Museum Visitors

A small museum of printing wanted to learn how visitors understood its exhibits. The staff had counted ticket sales for years, but the figures said little about what people noticed after entering. They decided to invite visitors to take part in short conversations at the end of their visit. Participation was voluntary, and the interviewer asked about the experience before explaining the museum's own intentions. This order reduced the chance that visitors would simply repeat the explanation they had just been given.

Early conversations revealed that visitors often remembered the large printing press but overlooked the workers who prepared the type. The staff had placed information about those workers on a label beside a smaller case. Some visitors passed the case without stopping; others stopped but found the label difficult to connect with the press. The staff responded by moving the label closer to the machine and adding a sample of type that visitors could examine. They kept the original press in the same place.

The museum then spoke with another group of visitors. More of them mentioned the preparation of type, but the staff did not claim that the new display had caused the entire change. The groups were small, and different visitors might have had different interests before arriving. The interviews nevertheless suggested that the revised display deserved further observation. Staff also watched whether visitors paused at the sample, without recording names or private conversations.

One unexpected finding concerned the questions visitors asked. Several wanted to know who had selected the objects for display and what had been left in storage. In response, the museum introduced a short account of how the collection had been assembled. This did not answer every question about the past, but it made the process of selection visible.

The project changed the staff's view of evaluation. Visitor numbers remained useful for planning opening hours and staffing. Conversations offered a different kind of evidence: they showed which connections visitors made and which explanations needed more work. Neither measure alone described the whole visit, so the museum continued to use both.

items.stem: Why were visitors questioned before the museum explained its intentions?
options: To identify which visitors had already seen the printing press
To explain the exhibits before asking for opinions
To hear visitors' impressions before supplying an explanation
To ensure that all visitors agreed to join the conversations
items.why: 原文说先提问可减少访客重复刚听到的解释，即第三项。

items.stem: What did the museum change after the first conversations?
options: It moved the printing press beside the smaller case.
It moved a label and added a sample of type near the press.
It placed all information about workers in the storage room.
It replaced the voluntary interviews with ticket sales counts.
items.why: 原文说工作人员将标签移近机器并增加可供查看的活字样本，即第二项。

items.stem: Why did the staff avoid attributing the entire change to the new display?
options: Staff had not recorded the visitors' names or conversations.
The second group showed no interest in the preparation of type.
The original press had been moved to a different part of the room.
The groups were small and could have differed in prior interests.
items.why: 原文给出的限制是 groups were small，访客原有兴趣也可能不同，即第四项。

items.stem: What prompted the museum to explain how its collection was assembled?
options: Visitors asked about the selection and storage of objects.
Staff found that visitors overlooked the workers who prepared type.
Staff discovered that all labels were difficult to read.
Staff needed a new way to count visitors at the entrance.
items.why: 原文说几名访客询问展品由谁挑选及哪些物品留在库房，博物馆因此补充收藏形成的说明。

items.stem: What is the passage's main point about museum evaluation?
options: Ticket sales can reveal every connection visitors make.
Interviews should replace all counts used for planning.
Different kinds of evidence show different parts of a visit.
Small interviews can establish the cause of every display effect.
items.why: 末段比较人数统计与访谈的用途，指出两者提供不同证据，即第三项。
